subtype: Restless at work and searching for stimulation [Actor]
passage: You want to know the real reason I asked for that new project, Nitin? Last year at the bank I had the same five reconciliations every morning. Done by eleven. After that I'd refresh the news, rearrange my desktop icons, make tea I didn't want, walk to the printer for nothing. By evening I'd feel this low, sticky guilt, like I'd stolen a salary. I thought I was just lazy. Then one day my manager handed me a messy data problem nobody else wanted, and I didn't look at my phone for three hours. I wasn't lazy. I was starving for something hard. So I asked for more of that. On weeks when I'm properly tired, though, I take the afternoon slow. Different hunger. Anyway, that's Varun's big secret.

qa.q: By what time did Varun finish the five reconciliations?
qa.a: By eleven.

qa.q: Why did Varun feel a low, sticky guilt by evening?
qa.a: Filling the hours with small distractions felt like not earning the salary, and Varun blamed laziness, not yet seeing that the work was simply too easy.

qa.q: What choice turned Varun's boredom into energy?
qa.a: Asking for more hard problems after noticing three focused hours on the messy data, while resting instead on weeks of real tiredness.

qa.q: How might Varun's manager see the change after the messy data problem?
qa.a: The manager probably sees an employee who was coasting become eager and focused, and may be glad to have someone who wants the tough work.

grounding: An under-challenged adult fills workdays with small distractions and guilt, then finds the boredom was asking for difficulty.

subtype: Restless at work and searching for stimulation [Actor]
passage: I'm Pankaj, and Hrithik sits two desks from me at the logistics office. For the last month I've watched him do something odd. He finishes his tracking sheet by noon, then spends the afternoon on small things: lining up every pen, checking cricket scores, walking to the pantry four times, rereading old emails. He jokes loudly, but when the boss walks past he quickly opens a spreadsheet and looks guilty. I'm not sure what's going on with him. Maybe he's tired, maybe he's bored out of his mind. Last Friday I asked him, lightly, "Too little work, or too little sleep?" He thought for a while. "Too little that matters," he said. On Monday he asked the boss if he could take on planning the new warehouse routes.

qa.q: What does Hrithik finish by noon?
qa.a: His tracking sheet.

qa.q: What does Hrithik's guilty look when the boss passes suggest?
qa.a: He seems to feel he is wasting paid time; the distractions don't satisfy him, and he is uneasy about being seen filling the day with nothing.

qa.q: Which question helped Hrithik work out what his boredom needed?
qa.a: Pankaj's light "too little work, or too little sleep?", which let Hrithik name the real gap, work that matters, and then ask for the route planning.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see Hrithik's afternoons, and what can't Pankaj be sure of?
qa.a: Pankaj sees the pens, pantry trips and loud jokes, but can't tell from outside whether Hrithik is tired or bored until he answers the question.

grounding: A colleague observes an unchallenged worker filling afternoons with small distractions and guilt until he asks for meaningful work.

subtype: Restless at work and searching for stimulation [Actor]
passage:
Monday: At the design studio, Nitin clicked between six tabs, none of them his poster brief: shopping sites, a quiz, a blog about bikes. He felt restless and guilty and blamed the dull project. Hafsa, at the next desk, noticed he'd yawned eleven times before lunch.
Wednesday: "When did you last sleep properly?" Hafsa asked. Nitin counted back. His cousin's wedding, two late nights, a long Sunday drive. "Maybe the poster isn't boring," she said. "Maybe you're just empty."
Saturday: Nitin slept till nine, went for a slow walk and didn't open his laptop.
The next Monday he opened the poster brief first thing. It was the same brief. But it held him for two hours, and he didn't open a single other tab.

qa.q: How many times had Nitin yawned before lunch on Monday?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: Why did Nitin blame the poster project for his restlessness?
qa.a: Restlessness felt like boredom, and the brief was the obvious target; he didn't notice that his tiredness after the wedding was the real cause.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did Nitin choose after it?
qa.a: Hafsa's question about sleep; Nitin chose a restful Saturday instead of forcing himself, and on Monday the same brief held his attention.

qa.q: How does Hafsa see Nitin's week differently from how he sees it?
qa.a: Where Nitin sees a dull project, Hafsa sees an exhausted colleague, noticing the yawns and guessing he needs rest rather than excitement.

grounding: Across a week a restless adult finds that his boredom at work was asking for rest, not stimulation.

subtype: Restless at work and searching for stimulation [Actor]
passage: Payal, you say the new job is "fine" but you spend half the day tidying your inbox? Let me tell you about me at twenty-five. I'm your Vandana Mausi, and back then I was a clerk at the district registrar's office. I finished my files by eleven. After that I sharpened pencils, restacked forms, walked to the window, came back. I felt guilty all afternoon, as if I were stealing my salary. I thought I was lazy. It took me a year to see it wasn't one thing. Some days I needed harder work, so I asked to help with the old land records nobody wanted. Some days I needed a reason, so I started helping elderly farmers fill forms at the counter. And some days, honestly, I was just tired and needed a proper lunch break, not a fourth cup of tea. So ask what your restlessness is asking for.

qa.q: By what time did Vandana finish her files at the registrar's office?
qa.a: She finished her files by eleven.

qa.q: Why did young Vandana feel guilty all afternoon?
qa.a: With nothing real to do, she felt she was stealing her salary, so the small distractions seemed like a personal failing rather than a sign the work didn't stretch her.

qa.q: What choices helped Vandana once she saw that her boredom had different causes?
qa.a: She asked for the harder land-records work, helped farmers with forms for a sense of purpose, and took a proper lunch break on days she was simply tired.

qa.q: How might Payal look at the inbox-tidying after this story?
qa.a: Payal might stop calling it laziness and ask whether the job needs more challenge, more purpose, or more rest.

grounding: An elder recalls being under-challenged at work, filling the day with small distractions and guilt, and learning to answer boredom with difficulty, meaning or rest.

subtype: Restless at work and searching for stimulation [Actor]
passage: For six weeks Gautam's team at the insurance office had been frozen by a merger. No new projects could start until the two companies agreed on software, and nobody knew when that would be. Gautam, twenty-five, answered two emails before ten and then drifted: news, a crossword, reorganising the stationery drawer, three trips to the vending machine. By evening he felt oddly guilty and exhausted, though he'd done almost nothing. His colleague Nikita found him labelling folders that didn't need labels. "Same," she said. "I've started learning the new claims rules from the manual, just to have something hard to chew on." Gautam thought about it. The next morning he asked his manager if he could draft training notes for when the merger went through. The afternoon flew.

qa.q: What had frozen Gautam's team for six weeks?
qa.a: A merger had frozen the team.

qa.q: Why did Gautam feel guilty and exhausted though he'd done almost nothing?
qa.a: Drifting through small distractions left him feeling useless, and the emptiness was tiring in itself; it felt like his fault even though the freeze wasn't.

qa.q: What choice did Gautam make, and why did it help?
qa.a: He asked to draft training notes for after the merger, which gave him both difficulty and a purpose, so the afternoon flew.

qa.q: What does Nikita's 'Same' do for Gautam?
qa.a: It tells Gautam he isn't alone in the drifting, and Nikita's example of chewing on the claims manual hints that something harder might help him too.

grounding: An under-challenged adult stuck in a work freeze fills the day with distractions and guilt, then finds relief in harder, meaningful work.
